title: Climate game

description.x: Inequality is the heart of climate justice. This game puts it in the room. Everyone starts on one line, and by the end nobody is standing on it.

sequence.x: Give every learner a role card (Activity sheet below). Each card describes a real kind of life, almost all of them in India. There are 13 cards. Hand the same card to two or three learners in a large group, or leave cards out in a small one.

Learners keep their role to themselves. Give them a few quiet minutes to imagine that person’s day — what time they wake, what work they do, what the house is made of, who else is in it. They will answer as that person. There are no right answers; they use their own judgement.

Clear a space, or go outside. Line everyone up shoulder to shoulder, facing you. Read the 15 statements one at a time. A learner whose character would agree takes one step forward. A learner whose character would not stands still. Keep the steps roughly the same size — it is not a race. By the end the line will have broken apart. Then ask each learner in turn to say who they were. Ask whether they think they are standing in the right place compared with everyone else, and let anyone who wants to move, move.

discussion.x: Look at the shape of the group and talk about it. Who was pushed furthest forward, and in what ways is climate change already inside their life? Who barely moved? Why those people and not others? Is it fair?

Every role carries a gender. Ask learners whether the game would have gone differently if their character had been a man instead of a woman, or the other way round. The cards use male and female only, to keep the question answerable. Other descriptions can be used, and it is worth agreeing the words with the class first.

Then ask what else, apart from the weather, decided where a character ended up. Money. Work. Gender. Schooling. Whether the family could move. Whether anyone in it had a job that still pays when you cannot go to it. Some learners will reach for the pandemic here, and it is a good example — a shock everybody met, and nobody met on equal terms. Climate change never arrives on its own. It lands on top of whatever is already there. Let learners argue it out.

Read the scenarios out one at a time. A learner either takes one step forward or stands still.

1. Climate change has already made your everyday life worse in some way. 2. It has already cost you money, or made your life harder. 3. It has broken into your schooling, or your child’s. 4. You expect to change your work in the next ten years because of it. 5. You expect to leave your home in the next ten years because of it. 6. You expect to have to move to another country because of it. 7. You expect to be poorer in ten years because of it. 8. Your family faces the risk of going hungry because of it. 9. It is damaging the land, water or wildlife where you live. 10. Your life and your work put very little carbon into the air. 11. It is making it harder to get clean water for your family. 12. It is making you more likely to fall ill. 13. It will change your children’s lives a great deal. 14. It puts your life at risk. 15. You — the character, not yourself — would become a climate campaigner.
